title: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive

topics.title: Parliament: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha

learn.hook: India's laws are made in a Parliament with two Houses. Why two? Isn't one enough?
points: The Parliament of India has three parts: the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
Members of the Lok Sabha are elected directly by the people. 543 members are elected, one from each constituency, for a term of five years. The Lok Sabha can be dissolved earlier.
The Speaker, elected by Lok Sabha members, presides over the Lok Sabha.

The Rajya Sabha represents the states and union territories. Most of its members are elected by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, and the President nominates 12 members known for art, literature, science or social service. It can have at most 250 members.
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved. Each member serves six years, and one-third of the members retire every two years. The Vice-President of India is its Chairman.

example.q: Think it through: The Lok Sabha is dissolved, but bills still need careful review. Why is it useful to have a second House that is never dissolved?
steps: The Rajya Sabha continues even when the Lok Sabha is dissolved.
Its members change in batches every two years, so experienced members are always present.
It gives a second look at bills passed by the Lok Sabha.
It also lets the states have a voice in making national laws.
example.answer: A permanent second House gives continuity, experienced review of laws and a voice for the states.

learn.reallife: On TV channels like Sansad TV, you can watch members debating in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha are the same. Explain the difference to Gappu.
teach.praise: Two Houses, two jobs! The people's House and the states' House.
teach.nudge: Who elects the members of each House? Which one is never dissolved?

learn.hook: Every law begins as an idea written on paper called a bill. It must survive debates in two Houses before it becomes law.
points: A proposed law is called a bill. It can be introduced by a minister or by any member of Parliament.
A bill is debated, discussed in committees and voted on. It must be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
After both Houses pass it, the bill goes to the President. Once the President gives assent, it becomes an Act, a law.
A Money Bill, about taxes and government spending, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can only suggest changes and must return it within 14 days.
Parliament also keeps a check on the government. During Question Hour, members ask ministers questions, and they debate the government's work and budget.

example.q: Think it through: Why must a bill pass both Houses and also get the President's assent?
steps: Two Houses mean two rounds of debate, so mistakes can be caught.
The Lok Sabha speaks for the people directly, the Rajya Sabha for the states.
The President's assent is the final formal step.
These checks make sure laws are made carefully, not in a hurry.
example.answer: Several stages of debate and approval make law-making careful and include the views of people and states.

learn.reallife: Laws you have heard of, such as the Right to Education Act, began as bills in Parliament.

quiz.q: What is a bill?
quiz.explain: A bill is a draft law placed before Parliament.
quiz.mistake: Thinks of a shop bill

quiz.q: After both Houses pass a bill, who must give assent before it becomes law?
quiz.explain: The President's assent turns a bill into an Act.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Prime Minister signs laws

quiz.q: Where can a Money Bill be introduced?
quiz.explain: Money Bills start only in the Lok Sabha, the directly elected House.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all bills follow the same rules

quiz.q: Within how many days must the Rajya Sabha return a Money Bill?
quiz.explain: The Rajya Sabha can suggest changes but must return it within 14 days.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a common time period

quiz.q: What happens during Question Hour?
options: Members ask ministers questions about the government's work
quiz.explain: It helps Parliament keep the government answerable.
quiz.mistake: Does not know Parliament's role in checking the government

quiz.q: Once a bill becomes law, it is called:
quiz.explain: An enacted bill is called an Act, such as the Right to Education Act.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up parliamentary terms

quiz.q: Which is a main job of Parliament?
options: Making laws and keeping a check on the government
quiz.explain: Parliament is the legislature: it makes laws and holds the executive accountable.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the legislature with the judiciary or Election Commission

quiz.q: Who can introduce an ordinary bill in Parliament?
options: A minister or any member of Parliament
quiz.explain: Bills by ministers are government bills; those by other members are private members' bills.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only the government can propose laws

teach.ask: Gappu wants to make a law: 'Every bird gets a free nest.' Explain to Gappu how a bill becomes a law.
teach.praise: First a bill, then two Houses, then the President. My nest law has a long journey!
teach.nudge: What is a bill? Which Houses must pass it, and who gives the final approval?

topics.title: The executive: President, Prime Minister and Cabinet

learn.hook: The President is India's head, yet the Prime Minister runs the government. How do both fit together?
points: The executive carries out laws and runs the government. India follows the parliamentary system, in which the executive comes from the legislature and answers to it.

The President is the head of the State. The President is elected by an electoral college of elected members of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies, and generally acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
The Prime Minister is the head of the government. The President appoints as Prime Minister the leader who has the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha.
The Prime Minister chooses ministers, who are appointed by the President. The senior ministers form the Cabinet. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the Council of Ministers must resign. Civil servants, such as IAS officers, form the permanent executive that carries out decisions.

example.q: Think it through: What does 'collective responsibility' mean for the Council of Ministers?
steps: All ministers stand together for the government's decisions.
They are answerable as one team to the Lok Sabha.
If the Lok Sabha loses confidence in the government, the whole Council of Ministers must resign, not just one minister.
So the government must keep the support of the people's representatives.
example.answer: The ministers act as one team, answer together to the Lok Sabha, and resign together if it loses confidence in them.

learn.reallife: When the news says 'The Cabinet approved a new scheme', it means the senior ministers led by the Prime Minister took a decision together.

games.title: Match the role
pairs: Senior ministers who take key decisions
House to which ministers are responsible

games.title: True or false?
items: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President.
The President appoints the leader with majority support in the Lok Sabha.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Rajya Sabha.
It is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
The President is elected directly by all voters.
An electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs elects the President.
If a no-confidence motion is passed in the Lok Sabha, the government must resign.
It shows the government has lost majority support.
In a parliamentary system, ministers are drawn from the legislature.
Ministers must be, or become within six months, members of Parliament.

quiz.q: Who is the head of the government in India?
quiz.explain: The President is head of the State; the Prime Minister leads the government.
quiz.mistake: Confuses head of State with head of government

quiz.q: Who appoints the Prime Minister?
quiz.explain: The President appoints the leader who has majority support in the Lok Sabha.
quiz.mistake: Thinks voters directly elect the Prime Minister

quiz.q: To which House is the Council of Ministers collectively responsible?
quiz.explain: The government stays in office only while it has the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Rajya Sabha can remove the government

quiz.q: Who elects the President of India?
options: An electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs
quiz.explain: Elected members of both Houses and of State Legislative Assemblies vote.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the President is chosen like the Lok Sabha

quiz.q: What happens if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the government?
options: The Council of Ministers must resign
quiz.explain: Losing the House's confidence ends the government.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand collective responsibility

quiz.q: The Cabinet is made up of:
options: Senior ministers led by the Prime Minister
quiz.explain: The Cabinet is the inner group of the Council of Ministers.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Cabinet with Parliament

quiz.q: Which group forms the permanent executive?
options: Civil servants such as IAS officers
quiz.explain: Civil servants stay in service even when governments change.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ministers are permanent

quiz.q: In the parliamentary system, the executive:
options: Is fully separate from the legislature
Comes from the legislature and is answerable to it
quiz.explain: Ministers are members of Parliament and answer to it.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the parliamentary system with the presidential system

teach.ask: Gappu asks, 'If the President is the head, what does the Prime Minister do?' Explain India's executive to Gappu.
teach.praise: The President is the head of the State, but the Prime Minister and the Cabinet run the government. Clear now!
teach.nudge: Who runs the government day to day? To whom are the ministers answerable?
